strengths: DDOME addresses a useful problem: personalizing predictions for unseen federated clients without labeled adaptation data. Combining client-level expert selection with per-sample routing offers a practical way to limit expert downloads.
The reported results are promising across vision and text, including 95.7% on CIFAR10, 78.6% on CIFAR100, and 74.9% on Yahoo! Answers, exceeding the evaluated baselines.

The supplementary experiments provide useful breadth: Dirichlet partitions, overlapping anchor distributions, initialization and anchor-sampling ablations, incremental client populations, and comparisons with matched expert counts. The sensitivity to common-expert quality is particularly informative.

The system description, training losses, and pseudocode make the main mechanism understandable. The authors candidly discuss pretraining dependence, communication overhead, scalability, and fairness risks. No material ethical concern is apparent in the benchmark experiments.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is incorrect as stated. With x distributed as N(0, I/sqrt(d)) and unit-norm ground-truth experts, the zero predictor has loss at most m/(2sqrt(d)). For fixed m, this vanishes as d grows; both sequential optimization stages can only improve this bound, contradicting the claimed dimension-independent Omega(1) loss. Appendix J also applies a random-subspace bound to a space containing V*, without an assumption controlling its overlap with W*. These are substantive gaps in a central contribution.

Even after correcting the theorem, its setup addresses only experts-first training under frozen random routing, followed by router optimization with frozen experts. It does not establish the broadly claimed necessity of joint training or characterize DDOME's behavior. A controlled empirical comparison of joint and decoupled training is missing.

The evidence does not isolate discovery of specialization from the supplied anchor structure. The main quantity-based experiments construct label-disjoint anchors, assign each to an expert, and explicitly supervise routing toward that expert. The overlapping-label experiments help, but anchor dependence remains strong. Fixed-routing and anchor-only controls would clarify what joint training contributes beyond this supervision.

The headline comparisons raise substantial tuning concerns. For example, CIFAR10 FedAvg deteriorates from a 93% pretrained checkpoint to 58.4%, and Appendix B identifies learning-rate mismatch as one cause of baseline failure. DDOME also receives a different optimizer schedule in the text experiments. Documented per-method tuning and validation-selected checkpoints are needed to establish comparative superiority; the gain over the unchanged CIFAR10 common expert is 2.7 percentage points.

Reproducibility and statistical support are incomplete despite the reported basic hyperparameters. The manuscript does not provide a code/checkpoint link or a sufficiently detailed recipe for obtaining the crucial common experts. It reports no repeated-seed uncertainty, while several supplementary tables select the best test accuracy during training without describing a separate validation protocol. This particularly limits confidence in smaller gains, such as 80.5% versus the 80% common expert on EMNIST.

The relationship to closely related personalized federated mixture methods, particularly FedEM, is insufficiently established. Joint gate-expert optimization is already central to classical MoEs, so the novelty must be demonstrated more precisely through DDOME's routing and anchoring mechanisms. The k-means visualization in Appendix I does not establish superiority over learned mixture or clustered federated methods.

Communication savings from sending K rather than M experts are plausible, but the paper lacks measured accuracy-versus-bytes, latency, or memory comparisons accounting for the common expert and routing overhead. The main FedMix comparison already transmits two experts per client, so those tables do not directly demonstrate lower communication. Overall, the theoretical and evaluation gaps outweigh the promising empirical results.
